newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin appeals to Russians over tax, upaid wages.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin appeals to Russians over tax, upaid wages.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin made an impassioned appeal to Russians on Friday to pay their taxes and provide the government with enough money to give millions of workers their unpaid wages.

Yeltsin, who is in a sanatorium preparing for heart surgery, signalled his concern over the frustrations of people who have not been paid for months and the losses incurred by tax evasion by dedicating a seven-minute radio address to the issues.

Speaking clearly and coherently, he announced the creation of a special commission to ensure taxes are collected and appointed Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to head it, with Krmelin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais as his deputy.

"Payment of salaries and pensions is not only a question of politics and economy. It is also a question of conscience," Yeltsin, 65, who is due to have an operation in about two months to improve the blood supply to his heart, said.

"I may assure pensioners and the workers of budget sphere, policemen and servicemen. Pensions and salaries will be paid. I, as president, am confident of it," he added. He was apparently speaking from the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow.
Yeltsin dramatised his plea by drawing attention to Moscow scientist Vladimir Strakhov, who has started a hunger strike to demand funds for his physics institute.

"I am appealing to those of you who do not pay taxes. The fate of this 64-year-old academic is on your conscience. The fate of more than 100 million of our countrymen depends on how taxes are collected," he said.

The lower house of parliament met as Yeltsin was speaking to consider the government's austere draft budget for 1997 which many deputies say does not satisfy social needs or meet the needs of the under-funded armed forces.
Communist Gennady Zyuganov said on Thursday the government was breaking promises Yeltsin made during his election campaign.
"The budget doesn't correspond to those main messages which were in the (government) statement when (parliament) confirmed its appointment," Zyuganov, the runner-up in July's vote, said.

Dismal tax collection has curbed the government's ability to fulfil its spending plans, prompting protests by groups ranging from power workers to actors and fuelling suggestions that the disgruntled, cash-strapped armed forces could mutiny.
The opposition-dominated parliament was expected to return the draft to the government, which would than have 20 days to come up with new proposals.
Millions of Russians have not been paid for months, despite Yeltsin's promises to settle all wage debts in his successful campaign for re-election this year.
Failure to tackle an issue touching much of the population could further undermine the president's authority and increase discontent with hardships endured under market reforms.

Yeltsin has been out of the Kremlin with heart trouble for most of the time since he was reelected on July 3, prompting talk of a Kremlin power struggle in his absence. The opposition says the country is rudderless and in chaos.
Yeltsin hit back by vowing to get tough on officials blamed for not paying out wages or witholding tax.
"All those responsible for delays in the payment of wages and pensions will face tough and decisive measures," he said.
The new commission, to be headed by Chernomyridn, would take over duties performed by the customs and tax services and check that budget funds were being spent correctly, he said.

Ekho Moskvy radio sation quoted opposition communist leader Gennady Zyuganov as casting doubts that the commission would be effective. His party, the biggest in the lower chamber, has also indicated that it will oppose the draft budget.
